row.result: Haiku and Sonnet as bettors on round 1's 116 post-cutoff findings: Sonnet met the rule (Brier 0.168, -0.064 [-0.099, -0.028] against the good-news rule), Haiku did not (Brier 0.208, -0.024 [-0.059, 0.011] against it); mixed, scored 0. Sean's card event (both under 0.25) was met.
row.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Published work already shows that a model one tier down from the top forecasts research results about as well as the top one, and that much smaller models do worse. BrainBench (Luo et al., 2024, arXiv 2403.03230; Nature Human Behaviour) found that 7B models "performed comparably to larger models", while TinyLlama (1.1B) was "falling much behind the 7B models". SciPredict (arXiv 2604.10718, 2026) has Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 22.55% against Opus 4.5 at 23.05% and Llama 3.1 8B at 14.65%. Hewitt et al. (2024, working paper) found that accuracy "improved steadily and markedly across generations of LLMs". Ours agrees on the size pattern: Sonnet is not shown different from Opus (Brier 0.168 against 0.163; paired difference +0.004, interval −0.018 to +0.027) and Haiku is weaker (0.208; paired difference from Opus +0.044, interval +0.012 to +0.076). What we found in no paper is a test of a same-family smaller model against a publication-bias rule ("bet on the paper's good-news side") or a "which version flatters the paper" rater. Wen et al. (2025, arXiv 2506.00794) do not mention publication bias, and CUSP (Wu et al., 2026, arXiv 2605.22681) has always-No, chance and mean-date baselines but no publication-bias one; Jin et al. (2024, arXiv 2411.17595) found GPT-4o-mini predicting every clinical trial a success, a smaller same-family model collapsing onto a positive-outcome rule, but report no such rule as a baseline. So the result that Haiku beats a coin but is not shown to beat the good-news rule by the 0.01 margin, and that neither smaller model beats the flattery rater on round 2's items (a reported row), is new. Search: "smaller language models predict research findings model size", "BrainBench small models scaling", "LLM predict experimental outcomes publication bias positive-result baseline", "predict outcome of new arXiv papers after training cutoff Claude Haiku Sonnet", "LLM forecasting scientific results larger vs smaller models same family" on web search and arXiv, plus the full texts of 2403.03230, 2604.10718, 2506.00794, 2605.22681 and Hewitt et al., 2026-11-05; claude-opus-5-5 (a fresh subagent that did not run ss-b13).

row.result: With each BrainBench pair shown in both orders and the ratings averaged, on the items ss-b10 rated once, the 'which version is better news for the paper's idea' question picked the real abstract 77.5% [69.5, 85.0] on Haiku and 89.7% [84.5, 94.4] on Sonnet, above the experts' 63.4%; pass, unreplicated. Scored by both picks (auditor), Haiku 67.0% [61.5, 72.5]. Opus 97.6% on 41 items.
row.novelty_line: **Novelty:** new. No published work I found reports that a valence question ("which version is better news for the paper's own idea?") solves BrainBench or any real-versus-altered results task. BrainBench (Luo et al., 2024, arXiv 2403.03230, *Nature Human Behaviour*) ran local-context, swapped-sentence, zlib-perplexity memorisation, publication-date, calibration and GPT-4-item controls, and found "no indication that BrainBench was memorized". It tests no valence, positive-result or publication-bias shortcut, and neither do its follow-ups (Luo, Sun and Love, 2024, arXiv 2405.09395; Luo, Ramscar and Love, 2024, arXiv 2411.11061) or Wen et al. (2025, arXiv 2506.00794, which checks "superficial features like idea complexity"). Lee (2026, arXiv 2604.06236) is not this test, and it does not mention BrainBench, valence or shortcuts. It proposes, without running anything (§5.5: "does not include empirical validation"), three things. §4.1: give LLMs only the starting information of 200–500 completed ClinicalTrials.gov trials, ask for a probability of success, and score with AUC-ROC and with the probabilities given to failed trials, hypothesising that "LLMs systematically overestimate the probability of experimental success". §4.2: compare five context conditions (none, successes only, failures only, both, failures classified by cause), with a dose-response at 10, 50, 100 and 200 failure records. §5.3: correlate "the published positive-result ratio and the actual success ratio (obtainable from trial registries)" across medical subfields, plus a peer-review test on OpenReview. So this project's earlier statement that ours is "the test an April 2026 paper asked for" (paper/novelty.md finding 8, ranked replication 1) overstates the link. The swap-both-orders-and-average fix and the first-position pull are known: Zheng et al. (2023, arXiv 2306.05685) found Claude-v1 consistent on swapped order 23.8% of the time and favouring the first answer 75.0%; Wang et al. (2023, arXiv 2305.17926, Balanced Position Calibration) average the scores over both orders. LLMs swayed by favourable framing is in print in another form (Yun et al., CHIL 2025, arXiv 2502.07963, spin in medical abstracts), but not as a rule for picking real results. What is new is only the headline, a one-line valence question beating the 63.4% for experts on BrainBench, and it cannot be told apart from memory or plausibility. Search: "BrainBench" with shortcut, valence, positive result, publication bias, memorization, contamination, follow-up; "LLMs predict scientific results publication bias"; "LLM spin medical abstracts"; "position bias swap LLM judge"; general web search and arxiv.org abstract and HTML pages, 2026-11-05. Model: claude-opus-5-5 (a fresh subagent that did not run ss-b10c).
